# Unclaimed

The office of the transit lost and found is a long room under the station, lit by fluorescents that hum at a frequency just below a headache. I have worked here eleven years. People imagine I spend my days returning things, and sometimes I do. A woman's face when she sees her grandmother's scarf folded in tissue paper is a sight I will never tire of. But most of what arrives is never claimed.

There is a shelf for umbrellas — hundreds, black and plaid, and one shaped like a parrot. There is a cabinet for electronics, a drawer for keys, a bin for single gloves. There is a locked case for things of obvious value and a box for things of no value that someone might still want: a child's drawing of a horse, a grocery list, a funeral program with a photograph of a man mid-laugh.

Unclaimed things stay with me ninety days. Then they are catalogued, boxed, and sent to a warehouse, and eventually most are destroyed or given away. I am the last person who will ever look at them carefully.

A wedding dress came in once, found on the 11:15, still in its garment bag, a dry cleaner's ticket pinned to the hanger. We called the cleaner. No record. We posted a description. Nobody came. For three months the dress hung on the back of my door, and every morning I looked at it and wondered whether the wedding had happened, whether this was a spare, whether someone had run. I dry-cleaned it myself, at my own expense, so it would not yellow while it waited.

A man's whole life arrived in a suitcase once: photographs, letters tied with ribbon, a marriage certificate, a discharge paper. We traced the name. He had died the year before, in another city. His nephew had carried the suitcase onto the train and left it on the luggage rack and walked away. When we called, the nephew said, in a voice I still hear, "I don't want it. I took it so the landlords wouldn't throw it out, but I don't have room, and I didn't really know him." The suitcase sat beside my desk for a long time. I read the letters. I shouldn't have, but I did. He wrote to his wife in 1963: "The city is loud, but you are in it, so it is home." She was in the photographs. They had no children. The suitcase is in a warehouse now, in a box marked miscellaneous, which is the truest word I know.

People ask whether I take things home. Officially, no. There is a rule. But last winter a coat came in — a woman's wool coat, navy, hole in the pocket — and in the pocket a theater stub and a hair clip shaped like a star. I waited the ninety days. I called the theater. The show had closed. I looked at that coat every day and thought about my mother, dead six years now, whose coats I gave away too fast, in that first brutal month when you want nothing in the house that still holds a shape.

I took the clip. Only the clip. It sits on my desk, and when the light catches it, it throws a small star onto the ceiling that I am probably the only person who has ever noticed.

What have I learned from eleven years of other people's forgotten things? That people write their names in books and then lose the books. That the thing you grab on the way out the door is never the thing you lose. That grief makes people leave objects on trains — I cannot count the urns, the folded flags, the hospital bracelets that have passed through this room. That almost everyone who loses a phone calls it immediately from a borrowed one, and you can hear the relief in the ring. That people lose the same umbrella twice and are embarrassed both times, and I pretend not to remember.

And that most of what we carry is replaceable, and the rest is not, and you cannot tell which is which by looking.

Last month a boy came in, nineteen maybe, looking for a backpack. It wasn't there. He stood in the doorway a long time, then said, "It had my brother's hoodie in it." I knew before he said anything else that the brother was dead. You learn the grammar. I searched the warehouse records. I called three depots. Nothing.

He said, "It was just a hoodie." He said it the way people do, to make it smaller. I gave him numbers for the other terminals and a card with my name, and I told him things surface. Sometimes they do. Six weeks later a backpack matching his description came in off a bus, and I called him, and he arrived before I had finished hanging up. He put the hoodie on right there, over his clothes, and stood a moment with his eyes closed.

I don't always get that. Mostly I get the dress on the door, the suitcase in the warehouse, the parrot umbrella nobody will ever want and that I cannot bring myself to discard.

At the end of my shift I turn off the lights. The room goes dark except for the exit sign and, if the streetlight is at the right angle, the small star from the clip. I stand a moment in the dark with all of it — the gloves, the phones, the unclaimed photographs of strangers' dogs — and then I go home, taking nothing, or almost nothing, with me.

People think the job is about objects. It is not. It is about the moment after the doors close, that half-second when a person realizes, and puts a hand flat on the glass. I collect what is on the other side of the glass. I keep it safe. I wait.

Most of them do not come back. The waiting is the job. The waiting is the whole of it.

**Lost Property**

The office of the transit authority's lost and found is a long room with fluorescent lights that hum at a frequency just below a headache. I have worked here for eleven years. People imagine I spend my days reuniting the living with their belongings, and sometimes I do — a woman's face when she sees her grandmother's scarf folded in tissue paper is a thing I will never tire of. But most of what arrives here is never claimed.

There is a shelf for umbrellas, hundreds of them, black and plaid and one that is shaped like a parrot. There is a cabinet for electronics, a drawer for keys, a bin for single gloves. There is a locked case for things of obvious value, and a box for things of no value that someone might still want: a child's drawing of a horse, a grocery list, a funeral program with a photo of a man laughing.

The unclaimed things stay with me for ninety days. Then they are catalogued, boxed, and sent to a warehouse, and eventually most of them are destroyed or given away. I am the last person who will ever look at them carefully.

[continue with specific objects...]

A wedding dress came in once, found on the 11:15, still in its garment bag, with a dry cleaner's ticket pinned to it. We called the cleaner. The cleaner had no record. We posted a description. Nobody came. For three months that dress hung on the back of my door, and every morning I looked at it and wondered whether the wedding had happened, whether the dress was a spare, whether someone had run.

A man's entire life arrived in a suitcase once — photographs, letters tied with ribbon, a marriage certificate, a discharge paper. We traced the name. He had died the year before, in another city, and his nephew had taken the train with the suitcase and left it on the luggage rack and walked away. We called the nephew. He said, in a voice I still hear, "I don't want it. I took it so the landlords wouldn't throw it out, but I don't have room, and I didn't know him, really." The suitcase sat by my desk for a long time. I read the letters. I shouldn't have, but I did. He wrote to his wife in 1963: "The city is loud but you are in it, so it is home." She was in the photographs. They had no children. The nephew didn't want it. It is in a warehouse now, in a box markedmisc.

[Then a more personal turn — an object that connects to the narrator]

People ask if I take things home. Officially, no. There is a rule. But last winter a coat came in — a woman's wool coat, navy, with a hole in the pocket, and in the pocket a theater ticket stub and a hair clip shaped like a star. I waited the ninety days. I called the theater. The show had closed. I looked at that coat every day, and I thought about my mother, who has been dead for six years, and whose coats I gave away too quickly, in that first brutal month when you want nothing in the house that still holds a shape.

I took the hair clip. Just the clip. It is on my desk now, and when the light hits it, it makes a small star on the ceiling that I am probably the only person who has ever noticed.

[A meditation on what this work has taught]

What have I learned from eleven years of other people's forgotten things? That people write their names in books and then lose the books. That the thing you grab on the way out the door is never the thing you lose. That grief makes people leave objects on trains — I cannot tell you how many urns, how many folded flags, how many hospital bracelets have passed through this room. That almost everyone who loses a phone calls it immediately, from a borrowed phone, and you can hear the relief in the ring.

And that most of what we carry is replaceable, and the rest is not, and you cannot tell which is which by looking.

[A specific encounter — a live one, to break the meditation]

Last month a boy came in, maybe nineteen, looking for a backpack. It wasn't there. He stood in the doorway a long time, and then he said, "It had my brother's hoodie in it." I knew before he said anything else that the brother was dead. You learn the grammar of it. I searched the warehouse records. I called three other depots. Nothing.

He said, "It was just a hoodie." He said it the way people do, to make it smaller. I gave him the number for the other terminals and a card with my name on it, and I told him that things surface. Sometimes they do. Six weeks later a backpack matching his description came in from a bus, and I called him, and he was there before I'd finished hanging up, and he put the hoodie on right there in the office, over his clothes, and stood there a second with his eyes closed.

I don't always get that. Mostly I get the wedding dress on the door, the suitcase in the warehouse, the parrot umbrella that nobody will ever want and that I cannot bring myself to throw away.

[Ending]

At the end of my shift I turn off the lights. The room goes dark except for the exit sign and the little star from the hair clip, if the streetlight is at the right angle. I stand there a moment in the dark with all of it — the gloves, the phones, the unclaimed photographs of strangers' dogs — and then I go home, taking nothing, or almost nothing, with me.

People think my job is about objects. It is not. It is about the moment after the door of the train closes, that half-second when a person realizes, and puts their hand on the glass. I collect what is on the other side of the glass. I keep it safe. I wait.

Most of them do not come back. The waiting is the job. The waiting is the whole of it.
